linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton (LINC) complex, a structure that 
spans the NE and connects the nuclear lamina (NL) to the cytoskeleton. 
Some progress has been made to understand the molecular pathways acting 
downstream of the defective genes, however the roles of these proteins during 
myoblast development and differentiation are still not fully understood. 
Using quantitative western blotting and immunoﬂuorescence microscopy, 
we characterised the expression of EDMD associated NE proteins during 
myoblast differentiation in healthy control cells, and cells from CMD patients 
harbouring mutations in lamin A/C and nesprin-1. We show that emerin 
is more highly expressed in myoblasts compared to myotubes, and that 
potential isoforms of SUN2 are differentially expressed during myoblast 
differentiation. Lamin A/C expression levels are highly variable but appear to 
be dramatically reduced in older cell lines. Emerin is known to be involved in 
the regulation of myogenic signaling pathways that are important for proper 
differentiation or that initiate myogenesis, hence emerin expression may be 
elevated in myoblasts when emerin is required and reduced in myotubes when 
it may not be needed. Changes in the expression of integral LINC complex 
component SUN2 could be associated with its roles in nuclear positioning 
and movement. As lamin A/C expression appears to decrease with age, in 
combination with the effects of disease-causing mutations, this might result 
in augmented disease severity as the patient ages. Together, these ﬁndings 
provide some insight into the roles of these proteins during differentiation 
and should be considered when investigating NE-protein associated diseases.

EP .351 
Painful spasms during childhood: Stiff-person syndrome 
A. Curado , M. Rosário, C. Gonçalves, D. Silva, I. Conceição, J. Coelho, 
T. Santos, T. Moreno 
Hospital de Santa Maria, CHULN, Lisbon, Portugal 
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune neurological disorder 
characterized by a progressive axial and proximal limb stiffness and painful 
spasms. Reports of pediatric-onset SPS are scarce. We report and present 
the videos of a 10-year-old boy, born in Angola, with no relevant personal 
or family background. At seven years of age, he started having involuntary, 
painful, paroxysmal muscle contractions, lasting from a few minutes to half 
an hour, initially only in the legs, and later in the four limbs, masticatory 
muscles and neck, with progressive worsening and daily frequency. On 
examination, he presented muscle spasms triggered by sound. He had no 
associated stiffness or hyperlordosis and no other changes on the neurological 
examination. EMG ﬁndings were supportive of SPS with simultaneous and 
continuous ﬁring of motor units at rest and co-contraction of agonist- 
antagonist muscles. Serology testing for anti-GAD65, anti-amphiphysin and 
anti-glycine antibodies, both in serum and cerebrospinal ﬂuid, were negative. 
Phospho-calcium metabolism and ionic changes, as well as other associated 
diseases such as diabetes mellitus, thyroiditis or epilepsy, were excluded. 
The patient was initially treated with diazepam and baclofen but deteriorated 
with more frequent spasms and spreading to other body parts. After a single

course of intravenous immunoglobulin there was marked improvement of 
symptoms. Currently, he is clinically stable after one year of follow-up, 
with rare and less severe symptoms, under symptomatic treatment only, with 
cyclobenzaprine and carbamazepine. SPS is a diagnostic challenge given its 
rareness. As in this case, SPS in pediatric age is typically seronegative and 
may have a presentation with more distal muscle involvement. Treatment 
is based on symptomatic control of spasms and immunomodulation of the 
disease with intravenous immunoglobulin, although there are no pediatric 
prospective studies.

EP .352 
Ve n g l u s t a t , a novel brain-penetrant glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor, 
for GM2 gangliosidosis and related diseases: Phase 3 AMETHIST trial 
design 
M. Petrovic 1 , R. Zheng 1 , C. Canabarro 1 , P. Minini 2 , I. Batsu 1 
1 Sanoﬁ Genzyme, Cambridge, USA; 2 Sanoﬁ, Chilly-Mazarin, France 
The GM2 gangliosidoses, including Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff diseases, 
are autosomal recessive disorders caused by pathogenic variants of 
hexosaminidase genes A or B, resulting in insufﬁcient hexosaminidase 
activity. The consequent lysosomal GM2 accumulation leads to progressive 
neuromotor disability and premature death. No approved treatment exists 
yet. V englustat is a novel, small-molecule, brain-penetrant glucosylceramide 
synthase inhibitor designed to reduce production of the sphingolipid 
precursor glucosylceramide (GL-1), and is being studied as disease-modifying 
therapy for multiple diseases associated with pathogenic glycosphingolipid 
accumulation. AMETHIST (NCT04221451) is a Phase 3, multinational, 
randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of venglustat in adults with 
late-onset GM2 gangliosidosis (primary population). The trial will aim to 
include a group of 2–18-year-old patients with juvenile/adolescent-onset GM2 
gangliosidosis, and ≥2-year-old patients with GM1 gangliosidosis, saposin 
C deﬁciency, sialidosis type 1, or juvenile/adult galactosialidosis (secondary 
population). The primary population (57 planned) will be randomized 2:1 to 
receive once-daily oral venglustat or placebo for 104 weeks; the secondary 
population (up to 20) will receive the same venglustat regimen open-label 
(dosed by weight in < 18-year-olds). Endpoint design reﬂects US Late- 
Onset National Tay-Sachs and Allied Diseases Association study results. 
Primary endpoints are annualized rate of change in the 9-hole peg test 
and percent change from baseline to Week 104 in cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) 
GM2 (primary population) and changes in plasma and CSF levels of GL-1 
and disease-speciﬁc biomarkers (secondary population). Secondary objectives 
(primary population only) are safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and 
neurologic tests (change in 25-foot walk and Friedreich’s Ataxia Rating 
Scale). Safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics will be followed for 6 weeks 
after last dose.

EP .353 
Spinal surgery in neuromuscular patients: the experience of a UK 
tertiary paediatric centre between the years of 2003-2021 
I. Hughes , E. Whitehouse, H. Dashti 
Manchester University NHS Foun, Manchester, UK 
Scoliosis surgery in patients with neuromuscular disease is usually 
considered by the adolescent period, but given the complexity of care and 
increased risk of complications in these patients compared to those treated

for idiopathic scoliosis, appropriate selection of patients is paramount. A 
retrospective analysis of medical case notes of neuromuscular patients who 
underwent spinal surgery at a UK paediatric tertiary centre between the 
years of 2003-2020 was performed. Descriptive characteristics of 71 patients 
and data relating to type of surgery, complications, referral pathway and 
time to surgery were recorded. Complexity of case was indicated by factors 
such as need for long-term ventilation or non-oral nutritional support and 
existence of cardiomyopathy. The largest group within this cohort were 
patients with Duchenne Muscular dystrophy, DMD (n = 27), followed by 
Spinal muscular atrophy (n = 17), other muscular dystrophies (n = 7) and 
myopathies (n = 7). Mean age at ﬁrst surgery was 11.8 years, and the majority 
of patients were listed for deﬁnitive surgery (n = 51) compared to rod- 
lengthening procedures. Complications of surgery included wound infections 
requiring either intravenous antibiotics or washout, intra-operative and post- 
operative respiratory complications and post-operative need for inotropic 
support. Mortality associated with surgery was 1.4%. In total, 156 surgeries 
were performed with 21 extra anaesthetics needed due to the complications
